quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and select the exact spoken sentence.
quests.hint: Listen for the subject and the family members - is it 'he' or 'she', and what comes first?
quests.explanation: In fast speech, 'she has' blends into 'sheez'. The key detail is the order: 'brothers' first, then 'a sister'. Distractors swap 'he/she' or reverse 'brothers/sisters' - common mishearing traps.
quests.textToSpeak: She has two brothers and a sister.
options: She has three brothers and a sister.
She has two sisters and a brother.
He has two brothers and a sister.
She has two brothers and a sister.

quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and select the exact spoken sentence.
quests.hint: Focus on two things: whose dad is it ('his' or 'her'), and where does he work?
quests.explanation: 'His' and 'her' are both short unstressed words - easy to mishear. In rapid speech, the key is catching both the possessive AND the place. 'Hospital' and 'school' sound very different, but learners often miss the subject word.
quests.textToSpeak: His dad works at a hospital.
options: Her dad works at a hospital.
His mum works at a hospital.
His dad works at a hospital.
His dad works at a school.

quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and select the exact spoken sentence.
quests.hint: Listen for the subject ('they' or 'we') and the adjective - is the apartment small or large?
quests.explanation: In connected speech, 'they live in a' runs together as 'theylivina'. The adjective 'small' vs 'large' is the main difference. 'They' and 'we' sound similar when unstressed. Always catch the key content word - here, the size of the apartment.
quests.textToSpeak: They live in a small apartment.
options: They live in a small apartment.
They work in a small apartment.
They live in a large apartment.
We live in a small apartment.

quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and select the exact spoken sentence.
quests.hint: Listen for the color AND the object AND the location - all three must match.
quests.explanation: Beginners often catch the color ('red') but miss the object ('bag' vs 'box') or the preposition ('on' vs 'under'). In fast speech, short prepositions like 'on' and 'under' are spoken very quickly - train your ear for these small but important words.
quests.textToSpeak: The red bag is on the table.
options: The red box is on the table.
The blue bag is on the table.
The red bag is under the table.
The red bag is on the table.

quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and select the exact spoken sentence.
quests.hint: Listen carefully for the subject ('she' or 'he') and the clothing item.
quests.explanation: 'Green' and 'grey' are easily confused - both start with 'gr'. 'Coat' and 'hat' are different but easy to mishear at speed. Notice 'she bought' - the past tense '-ed' ending in 'bought' sounds like 'bawt' in fast speech.
quests.textToSpeak: She bought a green coat yesterday.
options: She bought a green coat yesterday.
He bought a green coat yesterday.
She bought a grey coat yesterday.
She bought a green hat yesterday.

quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and select the exact spoken sentence.
quests.hint: Focus on the number and the location - and listen for 'are' vs 'were'.
quests.explanation: 'Five' and 'four' sound very different, but many learners mishear numbers at speed. 'There are' (present) vs 'there were' (past) - the tense marker is one small word. 'Shelf' vs 'desk' are the location options. Catch all three details.
quests.textToSpeak: There are five books on the shelf.
options: There were five books on the shelf.
There are four books on the shelf.
There are five books on the desk.
There are five books on the shelf.

quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and select the exact spoken sentence.
quests.hint: Listen for the subject ('he'/'she') and the time - and notice whether it's past or present tense.
quests.explanation: 'Seven' and 'eleven' both end in '-even' and are frequently confused at speed. 'He gets' (present habit) vs 'he got' (past) - the tense difference is in one short word. Daily routine vocabulary is essential for everyday listening comprehension.

He gets up at seven every morning.

He got up at seven every morning.

quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and select the exact spoken sentence.
quests.hint: Three things to catch: the subject, the meal, and 'before' or 'after'.
quests.explanation: Meal words ('breakfast', 'lunch', 'dinner') are frequently confused at speed. 'Before' and 'after' are opposite in meaning but similar in length - a one-word difference that completely changes the sentence. Notice how 'before going' links into 'beforegoing' in fast speech.
quests.textToSpeak: They have breakfast before going to work.
options: They have breakfast before going to work.
They have lunch before going to work.
She has breakfast before going to work.
They have breakfast after going to work.

quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and select the exact spoken sentence.
quests.hint: Listen for who takes what transport and where they go.
quests.explanation: 'Bus' and 'train' are both common transport words. 'School' and 'work' are the two most common destinations in everyday English. In rapid speech, 'takes the' links into 'takesthe'. The subject 'she'/'he' is the first word - catch it immediately.
quests.textToSpeak: She takes the bus to school.
options: She takes the bus to school.
She takes the train to school.
She takes the bus to work.
He takes the bus to school.

quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and select the exact spoken sentence.
quests.hint: Listen for the adjective (cold/hot) and whether it's inside or outside.
quests.explanation: 'Cold' and 'hot' are opposite but both one syllable - easy to mishear. 'It's' (present) vs 'it was' (past) is a tense shift. 'Outside' vs 'inside' - the prefix 'out-' vs 'in-' is the only difference. All four are common beginner listening challenges.
quests.textToSpeak: It's very cold outside today.
options: It's very hot outside today.
It was very cold outside today.
It's very cold outside today.
It's very cold inside today.

quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and select the exact spoken sentence.
quests.hint: Catch the subject and the item needed, plus the weather condition.
quests.explanation: Weather vocabulary ('rain', 'snow') sounds similar at speed - both are short, one-syllable words. 'Umbrella' and 'jacket' are very different, but fast speech can make unfamiliar words hard to catch. 'We' vs 'they' - both unstressed subject pronouns.
quests.textToSpeak: We need an umbrella in the rain.
options: We need a jacket in the rain.
They need an umbrella in the rain.
We need an umbrella in the rain.
We need an umbrella in the snow.

quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and select the exact spoken sentence.
quests.hint: Identify the season, the possessive ('my'/'her'), and the tense ('is'/'was').
quests.explanation: Season names ('Spring', 'Summer', 'Autumn', 'Winter') are important vocabulary. 'Is' vs 'was' shifts from present to past - a tiny but meaningful word. 'My' vs 'her' - possessive pronouns are often unstressed and hard to catch in fast speech.
quests.textToSpeak: Spring is my favourite time of year.
options: Summer is my favourite time of year.
Spring was my favourite time of year.
Spring is her favourite time of year.
Spring is my favourite time of year.

quests.explanation: 'Coffee' and 'tea' are the two most common hot drinks - both frequently ordered. 'I'd like' (contraction of 'I would like') - this is very common in polite requests. In fast speech, 'I'd like some' runs together quickly. Catch each food word clearly.

I'd like some coffee and toast, please.

options: The restaurant opens at noon on Saturdays.
The restaurant opens at noon on Sundays.
The restaurant closes at noon on Sundays.
The restaurant opened at noon on Sundays.

quests.explanation: 'Salad' and 'sandwich' both start with 'sa-' - a classic minimal pair confusion. 'Soup' and 'juice' are both drinks/sides. 'He' vs 'she' - the very first word is the key. In a fast food order, missing one word means missing the whole item.
quests.textToSpeak: He ordered a salad and a soup.
options: She ordered a salad and a soup.
He ordered a sandwich and a soup.
He ordered a salad and a soup.
He ordered a salad and a juice.

quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and select the exact spoken sentence.
quests.hint: Listen for whose class, when it starts (or ends), and the time.
quests.explanation: 'Starts' vs 'ends' - opposite verbs that sound quite different, but at speed you might catch only the first syllable. 'Eight' and 'nine' are often confused - both are one syllable. 'Our' vs 'her' - possessive pronouns before 'class'. School time vocabulary is everyday English.

options: Our class ends at eight in the morning.
Our class starts at eight in the morning.

Our class starts at nine in the morning.

quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and select the exact spoken sentence.
quests.hint: Notice the subject, the item forgotten, and the verb - 'forgot' or 'lost'?
quests.explanation: 'Forgot' and 'lost' are both irregular past tense verbs describing similar situations, but 'forgot' means you didn't bring it, while 'lost' means you can't find it. 'Homework' vs 'notebook' - both school items. This is very common real-world English for students.
quests.textToSpeak: She forgot her homework at home again.
options: He forgot his homework at home again.
She forgot her notebook at home again.
She lost her homework at home again.
She forgot her homework at home again.

quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and select the exact spoken sentence.
quests.hint: Listen for the place, the floor number, and whether it's present or past tense.
quests.explanation: Ordinal numbers ('second', 'third') are frequently confused at speed. 'Library' vs 'office' - both institutional locations. 'Is' vs 'was' - present vs past tense. When getting directions, catching the correct floor number is absolutely critical.
quests.textToSpeak: The library is on the second floor.
options: The library is on the third floor.
The office is on the second floor.
The library is on the second floor.
The library was on the second floor.

quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and select the exact spoken sentence.
quests.hint: Focus on the transport, the direction verb ('leaves'/'arrives'), and the platform number.
quests.explanation: 'Leaves' and 'arrives' are directional opposites - critical at a bus or train station. 'Three' and 'four' sound similar and are often confused by listeners. 'Bus' vs 'train' - both common public transport. This sentence type is vital for real travel situations.
quests.textToSpeak: The bus leaves from platform three.
options: The bus leaves from platform three.
The train leaves from platform three.
The bus leaves from platform four.
The bus arrives at platform three.

quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and select the exact spoken sentence.
quests.hint: Listen for the question word - 'how long', 'how much', or 'how soon'?
quests.explanation: 'How long' (asks about time), 'how much' (asks about price), 'how soon' (asks about timing) - three different question types! 'Does it take' (present) vs 'did it take' (past) changes the tense. These question phrases are among the most common in everyday English conversation.
quests.textToSpeak: How long does it take to get there?
options: How long does it take to get there?
How much does it cost to get there?
How long did it take to get there?
How soon does it take to get there?

quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and select the exact spoken sentence.
quests.hint: Direction vocabulary: listen for 'left'/'right', and the exact landmark.
quests.explanation: 'Left' and 'right' are opposites - getting them wrong means going the wrong way! 'At' vs 'before' - the preposition changes when you turn. 'Traffic lights' vs 'roundabout' - different road features. Giving and following directions is one of the most practical listening skills.
quests.textToSpeak: Turn left at the traffic lights.
options: Turn left at the traffic lights.
Turn left before the traffic lights.
Turn left at the roundabout.
Turn right at the traffic lights.

quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and select the exact spoken sentence.
quests.hint: Listen for who is speaking, the type of pain, and the tense.
quests.explanation: Health vocabulary: 'headache' and 'stomachache' both describe pain but in different places. 'I have' (present) vs 'I had' (past) - the tense tells us if it's happening now or before. 'Feel tired' is a very common phrase for expressing how you feel at the doctor's or with friends.
quests.textToSpeak: I have a headache and feel tired.
options: He has a headache and feels tired.
I have a headache and feel tired.
I had a headache and felt tired.
I have a stomachache and feel tired.

quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and select the exact spoken sentence.
quests.hint: Focus on who needs to rest, what they need to do, and for how long.
quests.explanation: 'Days' and 'weeks' sound similar but mean very different recovery times. 'Rest' vs 'eat more' are different medical advice. 'She' vs 'he' - subject pronoun at the start. Medical English like this is essential for doctor's visits and everyday health conversations.
quests.textToSpeak: She needs to rest for a few days.
options: He needs to rest for a few days.
She needs to eat more for a few days.
She needs to rest for a few days.
She needs to rest for a few weeks.

quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and select the exact spoken sentence.
quests.hint: Listen for who gave the advice and what they said to do.
quests.explanation: 'Doctor' and 'nurse' are both medical professionals. 'Drink plenty of water', 'eat plenty of food', 'get plenty of rest' - three common pieces of medical advice. 'Said to drink/eat/get' - notice how all three use the same structure. This is reported speech - essential English grammar.
quests.textToSpeak: The doctor said to drink plenty of water.
options: The doctor said to drink plenty of water.
The doctor said to eat plenty of food.
The doctor said to get plenty of rest.
The nurse said to drink plenty of water.

quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and select the exact spoken sentence.
quests.hint: Catch the question word phrase and what item is being asked about.
quests.explanation: 'How much does' (present) vs 'how much did' (past) - one word changes the tense. 'Jacket' and 'sweater' are both clothing items - easy to confuse. 'Cost' and 'last' ask about completely different things (price vs durability). Shopping English is one of the most practical areas for learners.
quests.textToSpeak: How much does this jacket cost?
options: How much did this jacket cost?
How much does this jacket cost?
How long does this jacket last?
How much does this sweater cost?

quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and select the exact spoken sentence.
quests.hint: Listen for who is looking, what size, and what clothing item.
quests.explanation: Clothing sizes ('medium', 'large', 'small') are important shopping vocabulary. 'Shirt' vs 'coat' - both clothing items. 'I'm looking' vs 'he's looking' - subject change. In a real shop, this phrase is used constantly. The contraction 'I'm' sounds like 'aim' at normal speed.
quests.textToSpeak: I'm looking for a size medium shirt.
options: He's looking for a size medium shirt.
I'm looking for a size medium shirt.
I'm looking for a size medium coat.
I'm looking for a size large shirt.

quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and select the exact spoken sentence.
quests.hint: Focus on the item, the tense ('are'/'were'), and the time ('this'/'next' week).
quests.explanation: 'This week' vs 'next week' - a one-word difference that's crucial if you want to catch the sale. 'Are on sale' (now) vs 'were on sale' (past) - the verb tense. 'Shoes' and 'bags' - different product categories. Sale announcements use this exact structure in real stores.
quests.textToSpeak: The shoes are on sale this week.
options: The bags are on sale this week.
The shoes are on sale this week.
The shoes are on sale next week.
The shoes were on sale this week.

quests.hint: Notice the subject, the hobby verb, and the tense - 'loves' or 'loved'?
quests.explanation: 'Read' and 'write' are both literacy activities but completely different hobbies. 'Loves' (present habit) vs 'loved' (past - perhaps she no longer does it). 'She' vs 'he' - the subject pronoun. Talking about hobbies and free time is essential conversational English.
quests.textToSpeak: She loves to read books in her free time.
options: He loves to read books in his free time.
She loves to write books in her free time.
She loved to read books in her free time.
She loves to read books in her free time.

quests.instruction: Listen to the audio and select the exact spoken sentence.
quests.hint: Listen for who plays, what sport, and which day of the week.
quests.explanation: 'Tennis' and 'football' are both sports but very different. 'Saturday' and 'Sunday' are adjacent days and easily confused. 'We' vs 'they' - a small but important difference. Sports and leisure vocabulary is central to everyday social English conversation.

options: They play tennis every Saturday afternoon.

We play tennis every Saturday afternoon.
We play tennis every Sunday afternoon.

quests.hint: Three details to catch: who, which instrument, and how long ago.
quests.explanation: 'Guitar' and 'piano' - both instruments but completely different sounds. 'Months' vs 'years' - a massive time difference in one word. 'He' vs 'she' - the subject. 'Six months ago' is a very common time expression in English. Past tense with 'ago' tells us when something started.

options: He started learning guitar six months ago.
He started learning piano six months ago.
He started learning guitar six years ago.
She started learning guitar six months ago.
